title: The four Labour Codes come into force
author: Editorial Desk
summary: On 21 November 2025 the Government brought the Codes into effect. BMS welcomed the move and called it support for workers.
body:
*Photo: BMS welcomes implementation of the Labour Codes*

After years of waiting, the Government of India announced on **21 November 2025** that the four Labour Codes had come into force: the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (the OSH Code). The step ends a long period in which the Codes had been passed by Parliament but not brought into effect. This post explains what the Codes are, what changes for workers, what BMS has said, and what is still to come.

## Background: from 29 laws to four Codes

India's labour law had grown over many decades into a large collection of separate Acts, each with its own definitions, thresholds, registers and returns. The Ministry of Labour and Employment's release of 21 November 2025 says that the four Codes consolidate **29 existing central labour laws**. The Code on Wages was enacted in 2019, and the other three in 2020. The aim stated by the Government is to simplify the structure, reduce duplication and extend protection to more workers.

The four Codes cover these areas:

- **Code on Wages, 2019:** a single definition of wages, minimum wages and timely payment of wages.
- **Industrial Relations Code, 2020:** trade unions, standing orders, dispute resolution, strikes and lay-offs, retrenchment and closure.
- **Code on Social Security, 2020:** provident fund, insurance, gratuity, maternity benefit and schemes for unorganised, gig and platform workers.
- **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020:** safety, health, working hours and welfare in factories, mines, plantations, docks, transport and other establishments.

## BMS response

Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh **welcomed the implementation** of the Codes. On its website, BMS describes the Wage Code and the Social Security Code as historic and revolutionary, and it had been asking since earlier in the year that these two be implemented without delay. In February 2025, BMS Deputy General Secretary Surendra Kumar Pandey had told the press that the organisation supported two of the four Codes and had serious objections to the other two, the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code, which in its view needed to be revised; he also said that BMS would launch protests if the Codes were passed without consultation with the union.

The BMS position therefore has two parts. It welcomes the Wage and Social Security Codes, in particular because of what they offer to workers in the unorganised sector, and it keeps its objections to certain provisions of the Industrial Relations and OSH Codes. It has asked for talks with the central trade unions and for amendments. The reasoning follows the long-held BMS method: support what benefits workers, and press, through representation, for correction of what does not.

## What changes for workers

The Labour Ministry's summary lists a number of key changes. In plain terms they are as follows.

- **A statutory right to minimum wages for all workers**, with a **National Floor Wage** set by the Central Government, so that no worker's pay falls below a basic living standard. Under the earlier laws, minimum wage protection depended on whether an industry was on a schedule of employments; under the Code on Wages the right applies to all.
- **Appointment letters** for workers, stating designation, wages and social security entitlements. For a worker, this document is the first proof of employment and is needed to claim a wage or a benefit.
- **An annual health check-up.** The release describes free annual health examinations, with a specific mention of workers above 40 and of those in hazardous industries.
- **Recognition of gig and platform workers.** The Codes define "gig worker," "platform worker" and "aggregator" for the first time. Aggregators are to contribute **1 to 2 per cent of their annual turnover**, subject to a cap of 5 per cent of what they pay to these workers, to a social security fund. Workers register through an Aadhaar-linked identity so that benefits stay with them when they change platforms or states.
- **Fixed-term employees** are to receive benefits comparable to permanent workers, with gratuity payable after one year of service instead of five.
- **Women** may work at night and in all kinds of work, with their consent and with safety measures provided by the employer, and the Codes prohibit gender discrimination in wages.
- **Wider social security.** The Government's release says that social security coverage has increased from about 19 per cent of the workforce in 2015 to more than 64 per cent in 2025, and the Social Security Code extends coverage to unorganised, gig, platform and migrant workers.
- **Simpler compliance.** A single registration, licence and return system for employers, an inspector-cum-facilitator model of inspection, and industrial tribunals intended to deal with disputes more quickly.

## The points BMS has contested

The Industrial Relations Code deals with matters that are most sensitive for trade unions: the thresholds for standing orders, the conditions for strikes and lay-offs, and the treatment of fixed-term employment. The OSH Code consolidates a large number of safety laws, including those on mines, factories, plantations, docks and transport. BMS has said that both Codes contain provisions that it regards as against workers' interests, and it wants them changed after consultation. The Government, on its side, has said that the Codes would be accompanied by consultation on the rules, regulations and schemes, and that existing provisions would remain in force during the transition. These two statements leave room for the discussions that BMS is asking for.

## What remains to be done

The Codes are laws, and laws become effective on the ground through rules. The Centre and the State governments have to frame rules under each Code, and the details of many matters, such as registration, inspections, the way aggregators will contribute, the contents of schemes, and the working of the health check-up, will depend on those rules. For workers and unions, the practical steps ahead are:

1. Taking part in the consultations on the draft rules, at both the central and the State level;
2. Ensuring that the registration of unorganised workers is done properly, so that they are able to receive benefits;
3. Watching that the floor wage and the minimum wage are fixed at levels that reflect living costs;
4. Continuing the dialogue on the provisions that BMS regards as anti-worker, so that amendments are discussed with the central trade unions;
5. Raising awareness among workers, since a right that is not known is rarely claimed.

## For the reader

If you work in an establishment covered by the Codes, ask for your appointment letter and wage slip. They are your first proof of rights. Keep a copy of the letter, note your date of joining, and check that your provident fund and ESI details appear on the slip. If your employer is a contractor, check that the principal employer's name is also recorded. A union office can help you to find out whether your employer has registered and whether your contributions are being deposited. We will report on the exchange between BMS and the Government on the points of objection in a later post.
